title: How Tencent Built China's Everything App
summary: This video explores how Tencent grew from a struggling startup into a massive tech empire by creating WeChat, an all-in-one super app that dominates daily life in China. It highlights Tencent's strategy of copying and improving successful products, monetizing vanity and social status, and navigating strict government regulations.
key_points: Tencent's official mascot is a penguin, but its real-world mascot is a spider, representing its sprawling network across gaming, chat, social media, payments, streaming, cloud, e-commerce, and entertainment.
WeChat acts as China's operating system, handling everything from messaging and train tickets to doctor appointments and tax filing.
In 1998, Pony Ma and four college friends co-founded Tencent in Shenzhen, initially launching OICQ as a clone of ICQ.
Tencent's business strategy relies on cloning successful ideas, studying what works, and executing them 10 times better.
Instead of intrusive ads, Tencent monetizes vanity and self-expression through avatar cosmetics, VIP badges, and digital goods like QQ Show.
In 2001, Naspers invested $32 million in Tencent, a stake that later grew to be worth $250 billion.
WeChat Pay gained massive traction during the 2014 Lunar New Year by launching 'Red Packets,' linking millions of bank accounts overnight.
Tencent holds major stakes in global tech and gaming giants like Riot Games, Epic Games, Supercell, Krafton, Ubisoft, and Roblox.
The Chinese government exercises strict control and censorship over tech companies like Tencent, requiring complete alignment with state security and data sharing.
Tencent's 25-year journey teaches that vanity and identity monetize better than ads, and if you do not cannibalize your winning product, someone else will.
content: Two tech giants go head-to-head; Tencent taking on Google. >> You probably know Tencent is the company behind WeChat, the messaging platform here in China that now claims more than 1 billion monthly active users. >> Tencent has now joined the big boys ' club; they have officially replaced Facebook among the top 5 largest companies. >> We are well familiar with Facebook, Tesla, and Samsung, right? When we think of the world's most valuable tech companies, these are the names that come to mind. But there is one company that has surpassed these three global giants in market value. Hi, this is Praveen Simon, and you are watching Tencent. If you go out and ask 10 people on the road about this company, most of them will just give you a blank, confused look. That’s because Tencent doesn’t just make one product; it does everything. Tencent’s official mascot is an innocent , cute penguin wearing a red muffler, smiling at everyone. But in business reality, that penguin is not the accurate animal to represent Tencent. What would it look like if a giant, massive spider were hanging on a huge web? That spider is actually the mascot that truly represents Tencent. What do the eight legs of that spider signify? They represent many verticals like gaming, personal chat, social media , payments, streaming, cloud, e-commerce , and entertainment. Tencent has spread deep into almost every single digital industry. And its web is so strongly woven that once you step in, that’s it. That web wraps around your entire daily life and will never let you out. You might not directly notice the Tencent brand name. But the spider web will have touched you at some point through the games you play daily like League of Legends, Fortnite, PUBG Mobile, Clash of Clans, or services you use like Spotify, Reddit, or Discord . Deal over China; Chinese Tencent leading $ 8.6 billion stake in the maker of Clash of Clans, Supercell. >> However, in Tencent's home country of China, it is a completely different story; there, Tencent dominates people's daily existence. Tencent has achieved an impossible reality that Silicon Valley companies couldn't even dream of achieving. It’s "one app to rule them all." People in Silicon Valley are longing to see if they can achieve at least 10%of what Tencent has accomplished. There is an app, guys, called WeChat. Outside of China, they call it the " everything app." >> In China, it’s not just one super app. >> But in China, it is literally the operating system for 1.4 billion people . Almost everyone in the Chinese population uses this app, spending an average of four hours a day on it. Just think about that number. The total screen time we spend on all other apps combined is what they spend on a single app in China. Do you know why? Because it’s not just a chat app. Imagine mixing Facebook, Instagram, PayPal, Uber, Amazon, Tinder, YouTube, Spotify, Zomato, and Zoom, and packing them all into a single app with a single user profile—that is WeChat. In some ways, it's a standing for the internet itself. >> From turning off your morning alarm to booking train tickets, collaborating with office colleagues, scanning QR codes at shops to pay, booking doctor appointments, and paying electricity bills, people live their entire physical lives inside this digital walled garden . On the surface, it looks great, right? We don't need any other app; WeChat is enough. But there is a huge danger in this, guys . A single private company has your live GPS location, your complete bank transaction history, your private voice calls, messages, and not just that—your entire browsing history and medical records; every single digital blueprint of your existence is with that company. There is something even worse than this , guys. Should I tell you? Private companies like this in China can only survive if they are compliant with the government. In a survey related to privacy, Tencent received a score of zero out of 100. That is, Tencent got a zero in handling people's privacy. That's not all. You send a message to your friend. Let's say that message is against the government. Just a small message, a three or four-word message. Before it even reaches your friend, the message is automatically and instantly deleted. If even a small violation is triggered on a WeChat account, the account gets frozen. If it gets frozen, you can't buy food, you can't book a bus or metro, you can't pay your rent, and you can't communicate with your colleagues. You will digitally vanish from your society. Tencent didn't form such a massive empire overnight, guys. It started as a small startup in 1998. Pony Ma's goal was to create a chat app like WhatsApp is today. Starting from there, how did it transform to a level where it controls the daily lives of a country's people? How did this company, which was once unable to pay server bills and on the verge of shutting down, turn into a billion-dollar company? What was their distribution playbook that helped them ruthlessly destroy competitors? And most importantly, after Tencent became so powerful, how did it survive when the Chinese government itself, fearing that power, took massive regulatory measures? In this video, we are not just going to see the success story of a company. Guys, how a tech giant turned convenience into power and how that power captured an entire country. If Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, or Mark Zuckerberg walked past you, you would definitely recognize them. But if Tencent's founder and CEO Pony Ma walked past you, 99...no, 99.9%... You wouldn't be able to identify who he is at all. Pony Ma's real Chinese name is Ma Huateng. In Chinese,' Ma 'means horse, so they started calling him' Pony 'in English for fun. He is a massive introvert, guys. He doesn't come before the press and doesn't give speeches. He doesn't sit on a world stage like his arch-rival Jack Ma and tell stories while holding a mic. Pony Ma's philosophy is simple: Stay in the shadows, do the work, make billions . Note this point, your honor—not millions , billions. In 1998, in Shenzhen city, Pony Ma started Tencent along with four college friends. At that time, an Israeli software called ICQ was a huge hit globally on the internet for real-time desktop chat. Pony Ma and his team got inspired by that and launched a clone called OICQ in 1999. Cloning is in the Chinese DNA, right? But this is where Pony Ma noted a brilliant ground reality. In the Western world, everyone had their own computer. But in late 1990s China, there were only internet cafes; not everyone owned a computer. Now, the contacts in ICQ didn't sync; there was no cloud back then. Everything was stored only on the user's local computer. So, you might be chatting with your friends at one cafe. If you go to another cafe and open the same ICQ, your friend list won't sync. Just think about it. Now, you buy a new phone. Your contacts, apps, games, and data all sync in minutes on that phone, right? It's very easy. But at that time, the concept of the cloud didn't even exist. What does Pony Ma do? He stores the contact list on a central server instead of the local computer. No matter which cafe or system you log in from, your friend list renders instantly. Secondly, in 1999, there was no broadband; it was just dial-up connections. It would take half an hour to download 5 MB. This ICQ, the Israeli software, had a download size between 5 MB and 10 MB. Our guy came along. He provided an installation file with a download size of just 200 KB. Obviously, since ICQ takes time to download, people would just download Pony Ma's OICQ. These two things worked out amazingly well, guys. In year 1, they had 1 million users; by the end of year 2, they had 50 million users. College students and youngsters all started using OICQ, but this wild success had three deadly nightmares. Problem one: In China at that time, servers were terribly expensive. As lakhs of messages were sent, servers crashed and bandwidth costs skyrocketed . Problem two: Tencent had a zero business model. It was a model of "I give my app for free, I don't want revenue." If a new user joined, it wasn't profit but a loss, because server expenses would increase, right? Problem three: This was the problem that was going to end Tencent's career. One day in 1999, an envelope from America arrives at Pony Ma's office. When he opens it, it's from the American tech giant that acquired ICQ—AOL, I think many of you know them. It was a cease-and-desist legal notice sent by their lawyer. You have stolen the name ICQ and named yours OICQ. The letter stated that if you don't shut down this company immediately, we will file a case in international court. Pony Ma got scared. Because his bank account had zero balance, he hadn't paid server bills, and on top of that, there was an international lawsuit hanging over his head. Desperate, Pony Ma decided to sell the company to a local Chinese telecom operator. He went to sell it, thinking they would give him $ 60,000. But the boss of that telecom company said, "Are you asking for $ 60,000 for this waste of an app? I wouldn't even give a single dollar for this, get out first," and kicked him out . That rejection is what changed Tencent's destiny. The early stages of 2000. Pony Ma only had enough survival cash left for a few more weeks. Right when they were standing on the edge, American venture capital firm IDG Capital and Hong Kong's PCCW stepped in to invest 2.2 million. Just imagine, if that check hadn't been signed properly that week, Tencent would have been wiped out of internet history today. Do you know why? Right after they got the money, in March 2000, an important thing happened that you all know about. In March 2000, the dot-com bubble burst . The global internet market collapsed. Tech funding completely froze. Tencent was lucky to have dumped the cash in right before the crash. Next, to solve the legal issues, Pony Ma shut down the OICQ domain completely and rebranded the name to QQ. But the cash burn issue still wasn't solved. That was when, in 2001, an investment executive from the South African media giant Naspers came to see Pony Ma. He noticed something: "Why is QQ in every internet cafe?" "This QQ app is so popular." "They say it has so many millions of users." "Why shouldn't we invest in this?" and he invested 32 million dollars. Today, in tech history, this single deal is called the greatest venture capital investment of all time. Because this 32 million later turned into 250 billion dollars. Just think about it, where is 32 million ? And where is 250 billion dollars! Now do you understand why they call it the greatest venture capital investment of all time? But here, you should have had a doubt: how did so many people invest such an amount in a company that hadn't even seen a profit? Literally, QQ had no business model at all. The funding received was only used for the runway. What did they trust to invest? They trusted QQ's user base. It was enough if people just used the application actively. That was the only goal. If you reach that, the money will come on its own. QQ's user base touches 100 million. Only now do they think. We have so many users. But these users are all chatting for free. How can we ask for money from people who chat for free? If it were a Silicon Valley company, they would just look for money. "Put a banner ad inside the app." They would say, "If you install the banner ad feature, you can put ads and make money." But Pony Ma observes a path-breaking psychology. People won't pay to chat. But they will pay to show off and look cool in front of others. Basic psychology. There is that mindset of showing off to others, right? It's generally in everyone. To give a small example, why do you think Indians buy cars? To go from one place to another comfortably and easily? Definitely not; it's to show off to relatives, neighbors, friends, and enemies that "I have bought this car" and feel proud. Pony Ma used this same mindset. In 2003, Tencent launched a feature called QQ Show. The concept was very simple. A 2D digital character would stand next to your chat profile. Like it is on Snapchat now, you could put sunglasses on that avatar, give it leather jackets, and change to stylish hairstyles. You could use real money to purchase animated background scenes and apply them to that digital avatar. When you open a chat window with your friends, your custom avatar stands there in style. To today’s generation, Fortnite skins, PUBG outfits, and Valorant gun skins seem completely normal, right? But back in 2003, spending real hard-earned cash on digital pixels that didn't physically exist was an alien concept to Silicon Valley. Silicon Valley's logic was: build a service or product, show boring banner ads, irritate the users, and make money . Tencent’s thought process was completely the opposite, according to their senior executive. He said: "When you have hundreds of millions of users, the last thing on your mind should be to spam them with irritating ads." "Your priority should be keeping users happy and selling them self-expression, vanity, and social status—that’s all." Look at the financial economics. To stitch a real t-shirt, you need materials, labor costs, and delivery costs. But for a digital avatar's sunglasses, once you design and code it, whether 10 people buy it or 10 million people buy it, the marginal cost is zero—100%pure margin. You might ask, "Does this really work?" Well, it did. 95%of people were using the QQ app for free without paying a dime. Those 95%of people kept the app active and thriving. But the remaining 5%—the hardcore users —bought avatar cosmetics, VIP diamond badges, and contributed to Tencent's revenue. In just one year, the company, which previously had no business model and was losing money, became profitable. In 2004, they listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, and Pony Ma became a multi-millionaire. But now, Tencent had a competitor standing in their way. The biggest tech company on planet Earth : Microsoft, in 2004. Around 2005, Microsoft entered the Chinese market at full force with their MSN Messenger. Was there any resource Bill Gates didn't have? Was there any money he lacked? Was there any server he didn't own? Microsoft thought, "QQ is just a small Chinese company; we can easily swallow them up." But in ground reality, MSN crashed and burned. Do you know why? There are three reasons . First, MSN was a corporate and stiff software built for white-collar professionals in Seattle; it was very formal. Second, QQ was young and localized: custom animated emojis, local slang, stickers, an integrated music player like Hike or Telegram, and avatars, games, and files that transferred at ultra-fast speeds. So, everything that culture needed, QQ already had. Third, even on slow internet connections , QQ worked at bullet speed. But MSN was constantly disconnecting. Microsoft burned hundreds of millions of dollars and eventually packed up and fled China. After Microsoft was beaten, Tencent's true superpower was revealed. An unbeatable distribution highway. Pony Ma had set up a unique internal culture within the company. At Tencent, there wasn't just one specific R&D department. Thousands of engineers and product managers across the entire company would research the market like vultures. And they kept monitoring it constantly. If any startup in the market launches a new trend, game, or utility app and it proves to be successful, the Tencent team observes it, copies it, and plugs it directly into their QQ platform. Pony Ma has openly said in an interview : "I don't blindly innovate." "The smartest approach is to learn from the best example in the world and then surpass them with better execution." Do you know what kind of statement this is, guys? I don't just make assumptions myself. I watch to see if something works or not . I sit and observe. If something works, I copy it, and then I make it ten. times better and superior, he says. That's all there is to business, it's so simple. If a creator makes a great game, he has to struggle with marketing, right? But Tencent just copies that same game, sends a single notification on QQ, and overnight, 100 million users are ready to play it. Do you understand now, guys, why they invested heavily in apps that didn't even have a business model? If you have active users, the money comes on its own. This is why Tencent is known in the Chinese tech industry as the "Killer Copycat." Entrepreneurs used to tremble just hearing the name Tencent. But in 2010, this aggressive strategy led to a massive civil war. Meaning, a war actually happened within a country because of one company. In 2010, there was a popular free antivirus software company in China called Qihoo 360, guys. Qihoo’s founder, Zhou Hongyi, publicly made an allegation against Tencent. The allegation was that Tencent's QQ software was secretly scanning users' private hard drive files, browsing history, and personal data. Not only that, he released a special software called "QQ Privacy Protector" and showed live on screen that QQ was scanning user data. Tencent started panicking severely. They were being shredded by court cases and the media. And on November 3, 2010, Tencent took a ruthless step never before seen in tech history. An emergency popup appeared on the screens of 300 million users in China. "Dear QQ user, if Qihoo 360 is running on your computer, QQ will shut down immediately." "If you want to use QQ, uninstall the Qihoo antivirus right now." "You choose: do you want the antivirus, or do you want QQ to chat with your friends?" That was the popup. This isn't a movie, guys; this actually happened. Just imagine the madness; it was like two tech giants were holding an entire country's digital population hostage on their desktops. In internet cafes, offices, and homes everywhere, the users were at the peak of their anger. And look at the network effects. Even though the users were extremely angry at Tencent, they couldn't uninstall QQ. Do you know why? Because your family, your school friends , and your office work groups are all on QQ. In case you uninstall QQ, you would be isolated from your digital world. The public outrage reached all the way to the state government. The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology intervened and mediated, telling them not to fight. "Both of you, remain peaceful." They curbed them, telling them not to overdo things like this. The Supreme Court dismissed the monopoly lawsuit filed by QO; the Supreme Court itself dismissed it. >> The Supreme People's Court maintained its original ruling, stating that Tencent did not create a... >> Just think about how much the government cares about people's privacy. For Tencent, this incident was a brutal wake-up call. The media in China wrote that Tencent was "Public Enemy Number One." >> We can have competition. The market. " >> If we compete directly in every field and destroy every startup in the market , society will not tolerate us. We must change," Pony Ma thought. Tencent changed their playbook 180 degrees. That is, "Don't copy anymore, invest instead." That was the new playbook. Instead of copying startups and destroying them, give them capital and become a shareholder in that company. That is, the plan was to control them indirectly. But just when Tencent was implementing this strategy, the biggest technological tectonic shift in world history occurred . That is, the smartphone revolution. iPhone 2. Apple is going to reinvent the phone. And in that transition, the product that was going to destroy Tencent didn't come from the outside. It came from within Tencent itself. There is a natural law in the business world, guys. When a tech transition happens, the incumbent usually dies. Kodak died when digital cameras came, didn't it? Nokia was wiped out when smartphones arrived. Yahoo was destroyed when mobile apps came. In 2010, smartphones started spreading like a storm in China. QQ, which was designed for desktop PCs, was unfit for mobile screens. Pony Ma had a crazy idea. "Before some small startup invents a smartphone messenger and destroys our QQ dominance, we must create a product from within our own company that kills our own QQ." This was that idea. Silicon Valley analysts call Tencent's corporate culture a "shark tank." There is a shark called the Sand Tiger, guys. While still in its mother's womb, its eggs hatch inside. After hatching, the baby sharks start attacking and eating each other. Finally, the shark that comes out of the womb has eaten its own brothers and sisters and emerges as the strongest shark. Pony Ma set up that same gladiator system within Tencent. He created three separate internal teams and gave them budgets. He told them, "Build a killer messenger for mobile." And then, he let the three teams fight it out. The product that emerged was Weixin, that is, WeChat. Initially, WeChat was just a simple chat app. But they introduced two killer mobile features. Number one: "Hold to Talk" voice notes. Typing Chinese Pinyin characters on small smartphone screens is like torture . So, in WeChat, you could simply hold a button and send a voice message. Just like we have in WhatsApp now. The second was "Shake" and "People Nearby." If you shake your phone, you can connect with anyone else in the world shaking their phone at that exact moment. "People Nearby" allows you to connect and talk to strangers within a 500- meter radius. In just 433 days, the new app called WeChat (Weixin) crossed 100 million users. As the fastest-growing communication app on Earth, Tencent decided to cannibalize its own flagship desktop QQ to capture the mobile throne. But now, the next challenge was how to turn this chat app into the financial heartbeat of a country. Until 2013, there was only one unshakable king in China's digital payment market. Jack Ma, with Alibaba's Alipay. This Alipay ruled China’s entire e-commerce and digital payments with an 80%market share. When WeChat Pay launched, people were afraid to link their debit and credit cards. They wondered why they should link their bank cards to a chat app. It’s like how we think today, wondering why we should integrate UPI into every random app. In January 2014, during the Chinese Lunar New Year, something happened. In Chinese culture, there is a tradition of elders giving money to the younger ones in red envelopes. Especially during festivals like this. So, the WeChat team launched a feature called "Red Packets." You could put 100 Yuan in a college or family group and click "Drop Red Packet "; the 100 Yuan would be randomly split among the first five people to tap it. One person might receive 2 Yuan. Another might receive 58 Yuan. It would be received after being split randomly. It was like a lottery, and this lottery excitement went viral all across China. People started playing with these Red Packets in their group chats. During the holiday season alone, nearly 75 million Red Packets were sent. >> About 5 million people used it during that year’s festival, and the number skyrocketed to over 760 million last year. That's about half of China's total population. Do you know what the catch is? To transfer the Yuan sitting in your wallet—the ones you received through the Red Packets—to your bank account, you had to link your debit card to WeChat. In a single weekend, with zero advertising spend, millions of Chinese citizens connected their credit and debit cards to WeChat. Tencent won 200 million bank accounts during the festival. When Jack Ma returned from his vacation , he was shocked by the data, calling it a "brilliantly executed Pearl Harbor attack on Alibaba." After this, people started using WeChat Pay in many places. Just like we have GPay, PhonePe, or Paytm QR codes in shops, everyone from vegetable vendors and taxi drivers to luxury malls and even shops in remote villages started using WeChat Pay QR codes. You just scan and pay. That’s all it takes. So, this became a habit for the Chinese people. People got so used to it that cash almost completely disappeared. The entire physical currency of a 1.4 billion superpower was now flowing through WeChat servers, but Tencent's master plan didn't end there. Next, they wanted to bypass the Google Play Store and Apple App Store. They wondered why they should bother putting their app in someone else's store. In 2017, WeChat did something very important, guys. Mini Programs. Normally, to book a ride, you have to download the Uber app; if you want food , you have to download Zomato. If you want a ticket, you have to download a movie app, right? All this takes up phone storage. What does WeChat say? Don't download all these apps. They say WeChat will do everything. Many programs are ultra-light cloud apps . This is even in Telegram. If you are a heavy Telegram user, you would know. Each small mini-app is under 10MB, which launches inside WeChat in under 1 second . Need a train ticket? Scan a QR code, and the ticketing program opens instantly inside WeChat. Are you at a restaurant? Scan the QR code on the table, and the menu card will open in WeChat. After you finish eating, you can pay through WeChat Pay. Doctor appointments, traffic fines, tax filings, casual gaming, grocery shopping —all this happens without ever leaving WeChat. WeChat became an operating system inside an operating system. >> We created a real interconnected ecosystem with WeChat, especially with the smart solutions provided by WeChat. >> Apple and Google are afraid looking at this. They think, "Who is this? We are the monopoly. Do they even know what a monopoly is? They are teaching us a lesson." Because in China, people don't care if they buy an iPhone or an Android; the only screen they see 90%of the day is WeChat. But we must talk about the dark reality behind this convenience, guys. If you start a startup in China, you don't need to go to app stores. >> So you need to have two versions that will cost some 300 to 4000; it's a very large cost for startups like us. However, if we just want to develop the software in which WeChat has built-in programs, we would just need to spend around 10,000 on that. >> Just building a WeChat mini-program is enough, which means Tencent is the ultimate landlord of the Chinese economy . If Tencent bans your mini-program, your startup will collapse with zero revenue in a single second. Now we have come to the most chilling part of this video. Imagine, guys, you are in a private chat with your friend and send a message criticizing a government policy. A tick appears on your screen as if the message was sent. But that message is never going to reach your friend. The University of Toronto's Citizen Lab researchers reverse-engineered WeChat and demonstrated this silent filtering mechanism live. In accounts created with Chinese phone numbers, if you send sensitive political words, unapproved historical photos, or protest images, they get deleted in real-time. Even if you move abroad and settle in the US or Europe, if your account is registered with a Chinese number, those filtering rules will follow you. In 2016, the human rights organization Amnesty International audited the privacy and encryption policies of global messaging apps. Signal, WhatsApp, Telegram, and Apple were all on the list. But do you know what score Tencent got? 0 out of 100. Not even a single point; a complete lack of end-to-end encryption transparency. In China's legal system, tech companies must cooperate with the state security apparatus. There is no gap between private data and state security. I would say that in all of our other reports that we've done on applications looking at the client side we've discovered that the same keywords that trigger censorship also trigger surveillance and from that point on all your conversations are monitored. >> The government can read the messages you send in real-time. They can track your location in real-time. In a normal country, if your social media is banned, you can just delete Twitter or Instagram and be at peace. But in China, if WeChat suspends your account, you won't be able to buy anything at a store. You won't be able to book train tickets . You won't be able to interact in your office work groups. You won't be able to do almost anything. You won't even be able to access your bank balance. You will become a digital ghost in your own country and get isolated from physical society. It is because of this extreme privacy scrutiny that WeChat couldn't expand in Western countries. In 2020, the Indian government banned 59 Chinese apps, right? Do you know who was at the top of that list? It was our own WeChat. In the US too, the Donald Trump administration issued an executive order to ban WeChat. But Pony Ma had other ideas. If I can't spread through the app, so what? We have tons of money lying around; Tencent is China's second-most valuable company, with stakes in several US and video game companies, including Tesla, Snap, and Epic Games, the maker of Fortnite. >> With that, he takes the next step, thinking, "I can do anything." Tencent's billions of dollars are silently entering the global market. Tencent is embarking on one of the biggest and most aggressive shopping sprees in world history. Just look at this jaw-dropping portfolio . I think you all know Riot Games. They are the creators of League of Legends, 100%fully acquired by Tencent. Epic Games, the company that created Fortnite and Unreal Engine. They bought a 40%stake back in 2012. A 40%stake even before the word "Fortnite" became popular. Do you remember Supercell? The company that created Clash of Clans , Clash Royale, and Brawl Stars. Tencent has majority ownership in that company. Krafton, the company that created PUBG. Tencent has heavy stakes in it. And Tencent alone has the exclusive rights to build PUBG Mobile. Tencent has stakes in Ubisoft, which created Assassin's Creed, Roblox, and Activision Blizzard, which created Candy Crush, Call of Duty, and Overwatch. Not only that, Tencent has stakes in tech and media giants like Spotify, Discord, Tesla, Snap, and Universal Music Group. You might notice it. Tencent operates like an invisible emperor. In the gaming industry's total revenue, Tencent is the single largest company in the entire world. Tencent's gaming revenue is significantly higher than the individual gaming divisions of Sony, Microsoft, and Nintendo. They print billions of dollars with a single game, their home-grown mobile game, Honor of Kings. It was Tencent's Lightspeed Studio that optimized PUBG Mobile for smartphone screens and turned it into a global sensation. During 2020-21, Tencent generated 86 billion in annual revenue and 35 billion in pure net profit. With its market cap touching 900 billion dollars, Tencent was showing off in the world's top 5 most valuable corporation elite club. Everything looked unbeatable. But, right at that peak, Tencent took two massive hits. The first threat came from a young Chinese competitor. ByteDance. Tencent's entire empire was built on a single strength. The social graph. Users 'acquaintances— friends, colleagues, family—would all be on that app. "We have 1.2 billion users." Tencent thought no one could compete with them, but then along came Zhang Yiming, the founder of ByteDance, to challenge their arrogance by building TikTok using an interest graph and a recommendation algorithm. TikTok’s philosophy was: we don’t need to know who your friends are; we just need to know what your subconscious brain likes. Once it discovers a video you like, that's enough. I will show you many more videos just like that. You will become addicted. TikTok built a dopamine machine. Chinese youngsters have a feature called' Moments 'on WeChat. Instead of checking updates from friends , they started spending two or three hours watching short videos on TikTok. Tencent's user screen time began to bleed out. To strike back, Tencent reached for their usual playbook: the "copycat" playbook. They did two things. One, they cloned TikTok and promoted it within WeChat. Two, they blocked TikTok links, videos, and mentions within WeChat. But, for the first time in tech history , Tencent's copycat playbook didn't work . Do you know why? Because you can copy an interface. But, you cannot copy ByteDance's years of trained machine learning recommendation algorithms. That is ByteDance’s moat. I think those who follow my videos regularly know what a "moat" is. ByteDance is years ahead in the AI that understands user preferences; Tencent is doing all sorts of things, launching features like video accounts and channels, but ByteDance made it clear that no matter how big your network is, consumer attention can vanish in a heartbeat. >> But if you just look at the revenue numbers, it's becoming increasingly large—bigger than Tencent, bigger than Alibaba, and slowly but surely becoming the main player. The next problem came from the Beijing government. As Tencent grew globally, a major problem arose, guys. The basic principle of the Western world is free speech.
